title: Medium-Vessel Vasculitis: Polyarteritis Nodosa, Hepatitis B and Kawasaki Disease
summary: Separate polyarteritis nodosa from microscopic polyangiitis by the kidney and ANCA, see why hepatitis B serology is always part of the work-up, and learn what NT-proBNP and IVIG timing mean in Kawasaki disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 54 Hit 6 (polyarteritis nodosa definition and the MPA distinction), Hit 8 (Kawasaki disease: age, NT-proBNP, coronary outcome), Hit 12 (HBV as the classic PAN trigger) and Trap 5 (red-cell casts in a medium-vessel vasculitis), checked against Wolff 2023, Pașa 2023, Terrier 2020 (French recommendations), Hur 2017, Gaggar 2024, Lin 2015, Marchesi 2018 (Italian guideline) and Uehara 2012. Three qualifications: the reviewer’s “10–20% still develop coronary sequelae despite IVIG” conflicts with the Italian guideline (coronary aneurysms in less than 5% when IVIG is given within 10 days; 15–20% is the IVIG-resistance rate) (register flag rv-kd-coronary-after-ivig); the NT-proBNP cut-off of 235.2 pg/mL is one study’s value (sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.77) and cut-offs ranged from 98 to 260 pg/mL with no best value established (register flag rv-kd-ntprobnp-cutoff); and the reviewer’s “>1/3 of adult PAN cases HBV-related before vaccination” differs from the “up to 30%” in Pașa 2023 (register flag rv-pan-hbv-historic-share). Not taught as fact: the “proteinuria >2 g/day” threshold (no source read), the “>80% between 6 months and 4 years” window (sources give >80% or 88% under 5 years and a peak at 6–11 months), the 1.6:1 sex ratio, myocardial infarction in ~2%, and national incidence figures other than Japan 2007–2008. The 2012 Chapel Hill paper and the AHA 2017 Kawasaki statement were not read directly (not open access); the Chapel Hill PAN definition is taken from its quotation in Wolff 2023 and Hur 2017.

objectives: Define polyarteritis nodosa using the Chapel Hill criteria and distinguish it from microscopic polyangiitis by ANCA and renal findings.
Explain why hepatitis B serology is required in every suspected polyarteritis nodosa and how the HBV share has changed.
Interpret NT-proBNP in suspected Kawasaki disease and state the coronary aneurysm risk with and without timely IVIG.

scenes.title: Two medium-vessel puzzles
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two requests arrive. Patient 1: a 55-year-old man with weight loss, testicular pain, foot drop and new hypertension; ANCA negative; renal angiography shows microaneurysms; a note asks “PAN or MPA?”. Patient 2: a 2-year-old with 6 days of fever, rash and red eyes; the ward asks “Can one NT-proBNP cut-off confirm Kawasaki disease?”

cues.text: Two requests arrive. A fifty-five-year-old man has weight loss, testicular pain, foot drop and new high blood pressure. His ANCA is negative, and kidney angiography shows small aneurysms.
A two-year-old has had fever for six days, with a rash and red eyes.
Is the man’s disease polyarteritis nodosa or microscopic polyangiitis, and can one NT-proBNP cut-off confirm Kawasaki disease in the child?

props.label: PAN or MPA? · One NT-proBNP cut-off for KD?

scenes.title: Two medium-vessel vasculitides
scenes.altText: Two cards. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), 2012 Chapel Hill definition: necrotizing arteritis of medium or small arteries without glomerulonephritis, without vasculitis of arterioles, capillaries or venules, and without ANCA; segmental, transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis and microaneurysms; no granulomas; mean age about 51–54 years in large cohorts, male predominance. Kawasaki disease (KD): medium-vessel vasculitis with mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome in infants and young children; coronary arteries are the main target. Japan 2007–2008: 88.4% of patients younger than 5 years, peak incidence at 6–11 months, about 217 per 100,000 children under 5 per year; US studies: 75–80% under 5 years.

cues.text: Polyarteritis nodosa and Kawasaki disease are the two classic medium-vessel vasculitides. Both inflame the main visceral arteries and their branches.

The 2012 Chapel Hill definition calls polyarteritis nodosa a necrotizing arteritis of medium or small arteries, without glomerulonephritis, without vasculitis of capillaries or venules, and without ANCA. The wall necrosis can form microaneurysms.
Kawasaki disease is a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children, with fever, rash and mucocutaneous changes. Its feared target is the coronary arteries.
In Japan, eighty-eight percent of patients were younger than five, with a peak at six to eleven months. American studies put seventy-five to eighty percent under five.

props.title: Polyarteritis nodosa
lines: No GN · no capillaritis · no ANCA

props.label: Japan: 88% under 5, peak 6–11 months · US: 75–80% under 5

scenes.title: The kidney decides: PAN or MPA
scenes.altText: Two kidney cards. PAN kidney: disease of renal and interlobar arteries — stenosis, aneurysms, renal infarcts, hypertension (up to 35% of patients), micro- or macroscopic hematuria and mild proteinuria; glomerular involvement is infrequent and glomerulonephritis is excluded by the Chapel Hill definition. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) kidney: ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis (anti-MPO in about 60%) with pauci-immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis on biopsy. Urine card: red blood cell casts and dysmorphic red cells are generally considered markers of glomerular disease (caveat: RBC casts were found in 29% of biopsy-proven acute interstitial nephritis in one study). Hook answer: patient 1 fits PAN; red-cell casts or MPO-ANCA would point to MPA.

cues.text: In polyarteritis nodosa, the kidney is hit at the level of its arteries. Stenoses, aneurysms and infarcts cause high blood pressure, blood in the urine and mild proteinuria. Glomerular involvement is infrequent.
Microscopic polyangiitis is an ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis. About sixty percent have anti-MPO, and kidney biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing glomerulonephritis.

So the urine sediment matters. Red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells are generally taken as signs of glomerular disease, which the definition of polyarteritis nodosa excludes. One caution: casts were also seen in some interstitial nephritis.
Back to the hook. The man’s negative ANCA, testicular pain and renal microaneurysms fit polyarteritis nodosa. Red-cell casts or MPO-ANCA would push toward microscopic polyangiitis.

props.label: RBC casts + dysmorphic RBCs → glomerular (not PAN)

scenes.title: Lab work-up: hepatitis B and NT-proBNP
scenes.altText: Left: PAN work-up card — hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc), possibly HBV DNA, plus HCV and HIV serology, is necessary when PAN is suspected (French recommendations 2020). HBV-associated PAN is driven by HBsAg immune complexes and treated with antivirals plus short corticosteroids, with plasma exchange in published protocols. Up to 30% of PAN cases were once caused by HBV; with vaccination and safer transfusion it is now reported in less than 5%. Right: KD card — NT-proBNP meta-analysis (6 studies, 279 KD cases): pooled sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.72; study cut-offs ranged from 98 to 260 pg/mL; best cut-off not established; 235.2 pg/mL was one study’s cut-off (sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.77). Coronary artery aneurysms: 15–25% untreated, less than 5% with IVIG within 10 days; IVIG resistance about 15–20%.

cues.text: Every suspected polyarteritis nodosa needs hepatitis B serology: surface antigen, anti-surface and anti-core antibodies, with viral DNA if needed, plus hepatitis C and HIV tests.

Hepatitis B surface antigen immune complexes are thought to drive this form. Up to thirty percent of cases were once linked to the virus. With vaccination and safer transfusion, it is now under five percent.

For Kawasaki disease, a meta-analysis found NT-proBNP about eighty-nine percent sensitive and seventy-two percent specific. Study cut-offs ranged from ninety-eight to two hundred sixty picograms per millilitre, and no best cut-off was established.

Coronary aneurysms develop in fifteen to twenty-five percent of untreated children, but in fewer than five percent treated with IVIG within ten days. About fifteen to twenty percent do not respond to the first IVIG dose.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Red-cell casts in a medium-vessel vasculitis mean PAN” (✓ PAN excludes glomerulonephritis; casts point to a small-vessel process such as MPA); “NT-proBNP above 235.2 pg/mL confirms Kawasaki disease” (✓ cut-offs varied from 98 to 260 pg/mL across studies; NT-proBNP supports, it does not confirm); “HBV-PAN is rare now, so skip hepatitis B tests” (✓ HBV serology remains necessary in every suspected PAN because it changes treatment).

cues.text: Trap one: red-cell casts in a medium-vessel vasculitis mean polyarteritis nodosa. No: that definition excludes glomerulonephritis, so casts point to a small-vessel disease such as microscopic polyangiitis.
Trap two: an NT-proBNP above one fixed cut-off confirms Kawasaki disease. No: cut-offs varied widely between studies, and the test only supports the clinical diagnosis.
Trap three: hepatitis B related disease is rare now, so skip the serology. No: it is still required, because a positive result changes treatment to antivirals.

A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: polyarteritis nodosa attacks the pipes, not the filter, and may carry a hepatitis B passenger. Kawasaki disease aims at a small child’s heart pipes, the coronaries.

Where it breaks: polyarteritis nodosa can also involve small arteries, and the hepatitis B passenger is now uncommon. Red-cell casts are not perfectly specific for glomeruli. Kawasaki disease also involves small vessels and older children.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “PAN: ANCA-negative, no glomerulonephritis, always test for hepatitis B”, “Kawasaki: coronaries of young children; NT-proBNP supports, timely IVIG protects”.

cues.text: Polyarteritis nodosa is an ANCA-negative medium-artery vasculitis without glomerulonephritis that always calls for hepatitis B testing, while Kawasaki disease targets the coronary arteries of young children, where NT-proBNP only supports the diagnosis and IVIG within ten days keeps aneurysms under five percent.

props.label: PAN: ANCA −, no GN, always test hepatitis B
KD: child coronaries · NT-proBNP supports · IVIG protects

explanation.what: Plain language: some vasculitides attack middle-sized arteries, the ones that feed organs such as the gut, kidneys, nerves and heart. Polyarteritis nodosa does this in adults and can follow hepatitis B infection; Kawasaki disease does it in young children and threatens the heart’s own arteries. Scientific terms: medium-vessel vasculitis, polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), glomerulonephritis (GN), red blood cell (RBC) casts, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), Kawasaki disease (KD), N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), coronary artery aneurysm (CAA).
explanation.why: PAN inflames artery walls, so the kidney is damaged through narrowed or ballooned renal arteries and infarcts, not through the glomeruli; the Chapel Hill definition excludes GN, capillary vasculitis and ANCA. MPA is a small-vessel, ANCA-associated disease that inflames glomeruli, so RBC casts point toward it. In HBV-associated PAN, immune complexes containing HBsAg are thought to drive the injury, so antiviral treatment changes management. In KD the coronary arteries are inflamed; early IVIG lowers aneurysm risk.
explanation.measure: PAN: renal involvement in 15–75% of patients, hypertension up to 35%, renal insufficiency about 15%; glomerular involvement infrequent (Wolff 2023). MPA: anti-MPO ANCA in about 60% (Terrier 2020). HBV: serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc; HBV DNA if needed) plus HCV and HIV in every suspected PAN; HBV-PAN up to 30% historically, now under 5% (Pașa 2023). KD: Japan 2007–2008, 88.4% under 5 years, peak 6–11 months, 216.9 per 100,000 under-fives per year; US 75–80% under 5 (Uehara 2012). NT-proBNP meta-analysis: pooled sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.72; study cut-offs 98–260 pg/mL (Lin 2015). CAA 15–25% untreated, under 5% with IVIG within 10 days; IVIG resistance about 15–20% (Marchesi 2018).
explanation.differs: PAN (medium/small arteries, ANCA-negative, no GN, microaneurysms, HBV link) vs MPA (small vessels, ANCA-positive, pauci-immune necrotizing GN, RBC casts). PAN (adults, mean age about 50) vs KD (children mostly under 5, coronary arteries).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick PAN versus MPA from ANCA and urine findings, choose hepatitis B serology as the essential test in suspected PAN, and recognise that NT-proBNP supports but does not confirm KD and that timely IVIG keeps coronary aneurysms uncommon.

comparisons.title: Polyarteritis nodosa vs microscopic polyangiitis
comparisons.distinguisher: ANCA status and glomerular disease: glomerulonephritis or ANCA moves the diagnosis away from PAN.

comparisons.title: Polyarteritis nodosa vs Kawasaki disease
comparisons.distinguisher: Age group and target artery: adult visceral arteries versus a young child’s coronaries.

mnemonic.text: PAN attacks the pipes, not the filter — and may carry a hepatitis B passenger; Kawasaki aims at a small child’s heart pipes.
mnemonic.explanation: Pipes are medium arteries, the filter is the glomerulus (spared in PAN), the passenger is the hepatitis B test, and the heart pipes are the coronary arteries in KD.
mnemonic.limitation: PAN can also involve small arteries and HBV-related PAN is now uncommon; RBC casts are not perfectly specific for glomerular disease (seen in some interstitial nephritis); KD also involves small vessels and can occur in older children.

NT-proBNP performance comes from one meta-analysis of small studies with different assays and cut-offs.
takeaway: Polyarteritis nodosa is an ANCA-negative medium-artery vasculitis without glomerulonephritis that always calls for hepatitis B testing, while Kawasaki disease targets the coronary arteries of young children, where NT-proBNP only supports the diagnosis and IVIG within ten days keeps aneurysms under five percent.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with weight loss and mononeuritis multiplex is being evaluated for systemic vasculitis. Which finding most strongly argues against polyarteritis nodosa and toward microscopic polyangiitis?

options.text: Red blood cell casts in the urine with a positive MPO-ANCA
options.rationale: Correct. RBC casts are generally taken as a sign of glomerular disease, and the Chapel Hill definition of PAN excludes glomerulonephritis and ANCA; MPA is ANCA-associated with pauci-immune necrotizing GN.

options.text: Microaneurysms of the renal arteries on angiography
options.rationale: Incorrect. Renal, hepatic or gut microaneurysms on angiography support PAN.
Incorrect. Hypertension occurs in up to 35% of PAN patients from renal artery involvement.
Incorrect. A negative ANCA is part of the PAN definition, so it supports PAN rather than MPA.

questions.stem: Which laboratory test does the 2020 French guideline describe as necessary in every patient with suspected polyarteritis nodosa?

options.text: Hepatitis B serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs and anti-HBc), with HCV and HIV serology
options.rationale: Correct. HBV-related PAN needs antiviral-based treatment, so hepatitis B serology (with HBV DNA if needed) is essential before treatment, together with HCV and HIV tests.
Incorrect. The French guideline lists anti-GBM antibodies for a pulmonary-renal syndrome or rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, not as the PAN-specific test.
Incorrect. Anti-C1q is linked to hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, not PAN.

options.text: Nothing beyond ANCA, because HBV-related PAN has disappeared
options.rationale: Incorrect. HBV-related PAN is now uncommon (under 5% of cases) but not gone, and finding it changes treatment.

questions.stem: A meta-analysis of NT-proBNP for diagnosing Kawasaki disease in febrile children is best summarised by which statement?

options.text: Useful supporting test (pooled sensitivity about 0.89, specificity about 0.72), but cut-offs varied from 98 to 260 pg/mL
options.rationale: Correct. Lin 2015 pooled six studies and could not establish a best cut-off; NT-proBNP supports a compatible clinical picture.

options.text: A level above 235.2 pg/mL confirms the diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. 235.2 pg/mL was one study’s cut-off, with sensitivity 0.66 and specificity 0.77; it does not confirm KD.

options.text: Perfectly specific, so a raised value rules KD in
options.rationale: Incorrect. Pooled specificity was about 0.72, so roughly 28% of febrile controls were above the study cut-offs.

options.text: Useless, because levels are the same in KD and febrile controls
options.rationale: Incorrect. Mean NT-proBNP was clearly higher in KD (750–1511 pg/mL) than in febrile controls (47–199 pg/mL).

claims.text: PAN: necrotizing arteritis of medium or small arteries without GN, capillary/venular vasculitis or ANCA (2012 Chapel Hill, as quoted); microaneurysms; no granulomas; mean age about 51–54, male predominance; PAN and KD are medium-vessel vasculitides.

PAN kidney: arterial stenosis/aneurysm/infarct, hypertension up to 35%, hematuria, mild proteinuria, GN infrequent; MPA ANCA-associated (anti-MPO ~60%) with pauci-immune necrotizing GN; RBC casts generally glomerular, but seen in 29% of AIN in one study.
HBV serology (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc, ± DNA) plus HCV and HIV necessary in suspected PAN; HBsAg immune complexes; HBV-PAN up to 30% historically, now under 5%; antiviral-based treatment.
KD a medium-vessel vasculitis of young children targeting coronaries; Japan 88.4% under 5, peak 6–11 months; US 75–80% under 5; >80% under 5 overall.
NT-proBNP pooled sensitivity 0.89, specificity 0.72; cut-offs 98–260 pg/mL; no best cut-off; 235.2 was one study’s cut-off; laboratory tests only support a KD diagnosis.
Coronary aneurysms 15–25% untreated, under 5% with IVIG within 10 days; IVIG resistance 15–20%.
Reviewer’s proteinuria >2 g/day threshold; “>1/3 of adult PAN HBV-related pre-vaccine”; “>80% between 6 months and 4 years”; male:female 1.6:1; MI in ~2%; “10–20% coronary sequelae despite IVIG”.
claims.note: Not taught as facts; the coronary figure conflicts with Marchesi 2018 and the HBV share differs from Pașa 2023.

claims.text: Patients invented; vessel and kidney drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 54 Hit 8 says 10–20% of Kawasaki patients still develop coronary sequelae despite IVIG plus aspirin. The Italian Society of Pediatrics guideline (Marchesi 2018) gives coronary aneurysms in 15–25% of untreated patients and under 5% of those given IVIG within 10 days; the guideline’s 15–20% figure is the IVIG-resistance rate. The reviewer may be counting coronary dilation or late-treated patients, which the guideline does not quantify, so the lesson teaches the guideline figures (register flag rv-kd-coronary-after-ivig).

Ch. 54 Hit 8 presents an NT-proBNP cut-off of 235.2 pg/mL as distinguishing KD from other febrile illnesses. In the Lin 2015 meta-analysis this was one study’s cut-off (sensitivity 0.66, specificity 0.77); cut-offs ranged from 98 to 260 pg/mL with different assays and no best value established. The lesson teaches NT-proBNP as supportive only (register flag rv-kd-ntprobnp-cutoff).

Ch. 54 Hit 12 says HBV caused more than one third of adult PAN before vaccination. The review read (Pașa 2023) says up to 30%, falling to under 5%; the exact historical share depends on era and cohort. The lesson teaches the source figures (register flag rv-pan-hbv-historic-share).

morphology.note: No micrographs or angiograms; vessels, kidney and urine findings are schematic.

verification.notes: 6 claims checked against Wolff 2023, Pașa 2023, Terrier 2020, Hur 2017, Gaggar 2024, Lin 2015, Marchesi 2018 and Uehara 2012 (all read as Europe PMC full text); 1 pending (reviewer’s proteinuria threshold, HBV share, age window, sex ratio, MI rate and post-IVIG coronary figure). The 2012 Chapel Hill paper and the AHA 2017 Kawasaki statement were not read directly. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
